Issued at 211 AM CST Thu Nov 19 2026

Winds south of central MN have remained steady overnight while 
slowly turning more westerly. Gusts are generally ranging from 20-30 
MPH early this morning, though MKT is seeing gusts to 36 MPH. While 
skies are clearing, lows tonight will only drop into the low to mid 
40s due to the breezy winds keeping the boundary layer relatively 
mixed. Highs today will reach the low to mid 50s while breezy 
westerly winds continue into the afternoon. West-central MN will see 
the strongest gusts at around 30 MPH. Winds will slow significantly 
into Thursday night, allowing for better radiational cooling to 
occur (even with the increasing cloud cover). Lows Thursday night 
are forecast in the 30s. Patchy fog even looks possible early Friday 
morning over eastern MN and WI where radiational cooling should be 
strongest. However, the calm doesn't last long as a strong LLJ moves 
northeast through the Central Plains and into the Upper Midwest 
Friday. Guidance shows this LLJ developing in response a bowling 
ball upper-level trough crossing east over the western CONUS. 
Southerly winds will quickly strengthen during Friday as the LLJ 
moves overhead. Sustained values will reach at least 15 MPH for the 
entire area with southern MN likely seeing near 25 MPH by Friday 
afternoon. It is here where gusts look likely to near 40 MPH. Did 
debate going even higher for wind gusts over southern MN and nearing 
Wind Advisory territory. However, did not want to jump the gun just 
yet as we will have increasing clouds that could limit daytime 
mixing. Gusts elsewhere should reach at least 25 MPH. The strong 
southerly flow will drive strong WAA and cause highs to reach the 
upper 50s to mid 60s Friday! The warmest regions will be southern MN 
into west-central WI.

Rain chances will begin to increase Friday afternoon into Friday 
evening across the northern half of MN as a surface low develops 
somewhere over the Dakotas. The one thing that has become clearer in 
recent forecasts is the aforementioned upper-level trough's 
evolution as it ejects east of the Rockies Saturday into Sunday. The 
trough will become positively-tilted and break up into chunks of 
energy in the process. This will lead to periods of rain chances for 
differing areas over the Upper Midwest as the pieces of energy move 
through. The first being Friday afternoon into Friday evening across 
northern MN, as mentioned earlier. Then, Saturday over eastern MN 
and WI as a cold front pushes east. PoPs are currently highest with 
this round as the slabular natured forcing of the cold front should 
cause a preceding band of rain. Forecast models still have some
spread regarding where the heaviest rain occurs. The GFS is 
mostly to the east of our CWA while the majority of guidance 
continues to favor southeastern MN into WI. Rainfall amounts are
also in question, as the band of rain could not be as intense 
given the decreasing synoptic forcing. But, areas in the 
rainfall maxima could see upwards of 0.5". The cold front will 
pass east Saturday night causing a sharp drop in temperatures 
(much closer to normal) for next week. For Sunday, highs are 
forecast in the mid 30s to lower 40s. Some cosmetic snowflakes 
may be possible early Sunday over eastern MN and northwestern WI
as the trailing piece mid-level energy moves into the Great 
Lakes. Temperatures dip farther heading into Monday and look to 
then remain steady for most of next week. Highs are currently 
favored in the low to mid 30s while overnight lows will range 
from the teens to lower 20s. Regarding precipitation chances 
next week, split flow is forecast to unfold over the central 
CONUS with our region being stuck in "no-man's-land" between the
two jetstreams. Guidance keeps any stronger disturbances to our
south and north, which leads to lower predictability for precip
(and very low PoPs). We'll have to wait until we get closer to 
next week for greater confidence in precipitation chances. 
Mesoscale features will likely be of more importance, which are 
typically resolved closer to a precipitation event.
